sections.title: Start here
sections.body:
Dynamics is statics with motion added. Forces that do not cancel make things speed up, slow down or turn.

There are three ways in: follow position, speed and acceleration through time; balance force against mass times acceleration; or track energy from start to finish. Energy is usually the fastest when the question does not ask about time.
pitfalls: Using an energy method when the question asks for time, or a time method when it asks only for final speed.
Forgetting that friction acts against the direction of motion.

tips.from: Mark Mattson, FE Dynamics Review Session 2022
items: For a projectile, solve the vertical motion for time first, then use that time horizontally.
In a composite mass moment of inertia, the parallel axis distance runs from the axis to the centre of mass of each part, not to its far end.

bridge.plain: Dynamics is the study of things that move and speed up or slow down. A net force makes a mass accelerate; without one, it keeps its velocity.
core: Position, velocity and acceleration are linked: velocity is how fast position changes, acceleration is how fast velocity changes.
Force = mass × acceleration, written along one direction at a time.
Energy and momentum give shortcuts when forces act over a distance or over a time.
bridge.links: It rests on statics (free-body diagrams) and calculus. Stopping distance and banking of curves in transportation are dynamics problems.
bridge.exam: Check whether mass is given in kilograms or weight in newtons or pounds before substituting.

sections.title: Kinematics
sections.body:
Kinematics describes motion without asking what causes it. Position, velocity and acceleration are linked: velocity is how fast position changes, and acceleration is how fast velocity changes.

With constant acceleration, three equations cover everything. For a projectile, treat horizontal and vertical motion separately: horizontal speed is constant, and vertical motion has gravity pulling down. On a curved path there is acceleration toward the centre even at steady speed. Spinning bodies follow the same equations with angle, angular velocity and angular acceleration.
pitfalls: Mixing units, such as km/h with m/s^{2}.
Forgetting that deceleration is a negative acceleration.

example.problem: A car brakes from 30 m/s at 6 m/s^{2}. How far does it travel before stopping?

ideas.title: Braking on a grade
ideas.text: On a slope, gravity adds or removes g × sin(angle) along the road. For road grades the sine is practically the grade itself, so the change in deceleration is g × G. This is the grade term in the transportation formulas.

ideas.title: The subscript 0 is any known instant
ideas.text: The constant-acceleration equations work from any moment at which position and velocity are known, not only from t = 0.

ideas.title: Timing a projectile
ideas.text: Vertical velocity reaching zero gives the time to the top. Returning to launch height takes twice that. Use the time in the horizontal equation.

ideas.title: Rotation uses the same equations
ideas.text: Replace distance, velocity and acceleration with angle, angular velocity and angular acceleration. Arc length is radius times angle in radians.

ideas.title: Constant acceleration
ideas.text: With constant acceleration, velocity rises linearly, so the average velocity is the mean of the start and end values. Distance = average velocity × time, which is the area under the velocity-time line.

ideas.title: Projectile motion
ideas.text: Projectile motion is constant horizontal velocity combined with constant downward acceleration. On level ground the time of flight is 2 v sin(angle) / g, and the range is R = v^{2} sin(2 × angle) / g.

ideas.title: Normal and tangential components
ideas.text: Constant speed on a curve still means acceleration, because the direction of the velocity changes. The normal (centripetal) acceleration is v^{2} / r, directed toward the centre of curvature.

ideas.title: Constant acceleration
ideas.text: On a grade, gravity adds g times the grade to the deceleration when climbing, and takes it away when descending. With a constant total deceleration, stopping time is the speed divided by it.

examples.problem: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly to 36 m/s in 10 s. How far does it travel in that time?
examples.idea: With constant acceleration, velocity rises linearly, so the average velocity is the mean of the start and end values. Distance = average velocity × time, which is the area under the velocity-time line.
examples.steps:
Acceleration a = 36 / 10 = 3.60 m/s^{2}.

s = \frac{1}{2} a t^{2} = \frac{1}{2}(3.60)(10)^{2} = 180.0 m.

Check: average speed 18 m/s × 10 s = 180.0 m.

examples.problem: A ball is launched from level ground at 40 m/s, at 45° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, how far away does it land? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.idea: Projectile motion is constant horizontal velocity combined with constant downward acceleration. On level ground the time of flight is 2 v sin(angle) / g, and the range is R = v^{2} sin(2 × angle) / g.
examples.steps:
Time of flight = \frac{2(40) sin 45°}{9.81} = 5.77 s.

Horizontal speed = 40 cos 45° = 28.28 m/s.

Range = 28.28 × 5.77 = 163.1 m.

examples.idea: Constant speed on a curve still means acceleration, because the direction of the velocity changes. The normal (centripetal) acceleration is v^{2} / r, directed toward the centre of curvature.

examples.problem: A projectile is launched from level ground at 32 m/s, 48° above the horizontal. What maximum height does it reach? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.idea: Only the vertical component of the launch velocity carries the projectile upward, and at the top it is zero. The height is that component squared divided by 2g.

examples.problem: A wheel starts from rest and accelerates at a constant 4.2 rad/s^{2} for 6 s. How many revolutions does it turn in that time?
examples.idea: Rotation under constant angular acceleration follows the same equations as straight-line motion: angle = (1/2)(angular acceleration)(time)^{2} from rest. One revolution is 2π radians.

sections.deep:
Kinematics describes motion without asking what causes it. Position, velocity and acceleration are linked by differentiation and integration. With constant acceleration three equations cover everything: v = v_{0} + a t, s = s_{0} + v_{0} t + a t^{2}/2 and v^{2} = v_{0}^{2} + 2 a (s - s_{0}).

Projectile motion is two independent motions: constant velocity horizontally and constant acceleration g vertically, linked only by time. On a curved path acceleration has a tangential part (change in speed) and a normal part v^{2} / r (change in direction).
method: List the knowns and the unknown and choose a positive direction.
Pick the constant-acceleration equation that contains exactly those quantities.
For a projectile, write separate x and y equations and solve the one with a single unknown first, usually for time.
For curved motion, compute the normal acceleration from v^{2} / r.
Check signs and that times are positive.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: Kinematics describes motion without asking what causes it. Velocity is the rate of change of position; acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. With constant acceleration a few standard equations link distance, speed and time.
sections.work: Stopping sight distance is this topic applied: distance covered while reacting, plus distance covered while braking.
terms: moment
the turning effect of a force about a point: the force times its perpendicular distance from that point
symbols: acceleration due to gravity, 9.81 m/s^{2} (32.2 ft/s^{2})

sections.title: Mass moments of inertia
sections.body:
The mass moment of inertia is a body's resistance to being spun up or slowed down. It plays the role for rotation that mass plays for straight-line motion. It depends on how much mass there is and how far that mass sits from the axis.

The handbook lists values for common shapes about their centres. To use a different parallel axis, add the mass times the square of the distance between the axes.
pitfalls: Confusing the mass moment of inertia (kg·m^{2}) with the area moment of inertia (mm^{4}).

example.problem: A 4 kg rod is 1.5 m long. Find its moment of inertia about one end.

ideas.title: Like a composite area
ideas.text: A composite mass moment of inertia is the sum of each part's own centroidal value plus m d^{2}, with d measured from the axis to that part's centre of mass. The transfer term usually dominates.

ideas.title: Mass moment of inertia
ideas.text: For a slender rod, I = m L^{2} / 12 about its centre. The parallel axis theorem moves it to the end: I = m L^{2} / 12 + m (L/2)^{2} = m L^{2} / 3. Moving the axis away from the centre of mass always increases I.

ideas.title: Mass moment of inertia
ideas.text: For a solid disk or cylinder about its axis, I = m r^{2} / 2. A thin ring with the same mass and radius has I = m r^{2}, twice as much, because all its mass sits at the full radius.

ideas.title: Mass moment of inertia
ideas.text: Moments of inertia about the same axis add. Take each part about the pivot: use the tabulated value where the axis matches, and the parallel axis theorem, or m d^{2} for a small mass, where it does not. The distance d runs from the axis to that part's own centre of mass.

examples.problem: A thin uniform rod has a mass of 15 kg and a length of 3 m. What is its mass moment of inertia about an axis through one end, perpendicular to the rod?
examples.idea: For a slender rod, I = m L^{2} / 12 about its centre. The parallel axis theorem moves it to the end: I = m L^{2} / 12 + m (L/2)^{2} = m L^{2} / 3. Moving the axis away from the centre of mass always increases I.

examples.problem: A solid uniform disk has a mass of 30 kg and a radius of 0.25 m. What is its mass moment of inertia about its central axis?
examples.idea: For a solid disk or cylinder about its axis, I = m r^{2} / 2. A thin ring with the same mass and radius has I = m r^{2}, twice as much, because all its mass sits at the full radius.

examples.problem: A slender rod of mass 9 kg and length 2 m is pivoted at one end. A small 3 kg mass is fixed to its free end. What is the mass moment of inertia of the assembly about the pivot?
examples.idea: Moments of inertia about the same axis add. Take each part about the pivot: use the tabulated value where the axis matches, and the parallel axis theorem, or m d^{2} for a small mass, where it does not. The distance d runs from the axis to that part's own centre of mass.
examples.steps:
Rod about its end: \frac{9(2)^{2}}{3} = 12.00 kg·m^{2}.

Tip mass, treated as a particle 2 m from the pivot: 3(2)^{2} = 12.00 kg·m^{2}.

Total = 12.00 + 12.00 = 24.00 kg·m^{2}.

examples.problem: A hollow cylinder has a mass of 29 kg, an outer radius of 0.33 m and an inner radius of 0.20 m. What is its mass moment of inertia about its central axis?
examples.idea: For a hollow cylinder about its own axis, I = m(r_{o}^{2} + r_{i}^{2}) / 2. The radii are added, not subtracted, because for a given mass a hollow shape has its material farther from the axis than a solid one.

examples.problem: A rotor has a mass of 29 kg and a mass moment of inertia of 9.2 kg·m^{2} about its axis. What is its radius of gyration?
examples.idea: The radius of gyration is the distance from the axis at which all the mass could be concentrated to give the same moment of inertia: I = m k^{2}.

examples.problem: A solid uniform disk has a mass of 14 kg and a radius of 0.3 m. What is its mass moment of inertia about an axis through its rim, perpendicular to the disk?
examples.idea: The parallel axis theorem moves a moment of inertia from the centre of mass to a parallel axis: add the mass times the square of the distance between the axes. For a disk about its rim that gives m r^{2} / 2 + m r^{2}.

sections.deep:
The mass moment of inertia is a body's resistance to angular acceleration, the rotational counterpart of mass. It depends on how far the mass sits from the axis, with distance squared, so a ring has twice the inertia of a solid disk of the same mass and radius.

The handbook tabulates it for common bodies about their centres of mass. The parallel axis theorem, I = I about the centre of mass + m d^{2}, moves it to any parallel axis. Do not confuse it with the area moment of inertia used in bending; the units differ (kg·m^{2} against m^{4}).
method: Identify the body's shape and the axis of rotation.
Read the formula for the axis through the centre of mass.
If the axis is elsewhere, add m d^{2}.
For a composite body, add the parts about the same axis.
Check units of mass times length squared.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: A spinning object resists changes to its spin. The mass moment of inertia measures that resistance: it grows with the mass and with the square of its distance from the axis.
terms: mass moment of inertia
a body's resistance to being spun up or slowed down about an axis
moment
the turning effect of a force about a point: the force times its perpendicular distance from that point
parallel axis theorem
the rule for moving a moment of inertia to a parallel axis: add the area times the square of the distance between the axes
symbols: mass moment of inertia about the centre of mass
mass moment of inertia about an axis through the end

sections.title: Force and acceleration
sections.body:
Newton's second law says an unbalanced force makes a mass accelerate in the direction of that force. Draw a free body diagram exactly as in statics, but set the sum of forces equal to mass times acceleration instead of zero.

Choose axes along and perpendicular to the motion. Friction acts against motion and equals the kinetic coefficient times the normal force. For rotation about a fixed axis, the sum of moments equals the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration.
pitfalls: Using weight (N) where mass (kg) is needed, or the reverse.
Leaving out the component of weight along an incline.

example.problem: A 10 kg block is pushed along a smooth floor by a 40 N force. Find its acceleration.

figure.svg: <path d='M96 150 L304 150 L304 30 Z' fill='#EEEDE8' stroke='#00242E' stroke-width='2'/><g transform='translate(210 84) rotate(-30)'><rect x='-24' y='-30' width='48' height='30' fill='#D9F1D6' stroke='#1B795A' stroke-width='2'/></g><text x='140' y='144' text-anchor='middle' font-size='12' font-weight='400' fill='#00242E'>30°</text>
figure.alt: A block on an incline at 30° to the horizontal.
figure.caption: On a frictionless incline only the weight component along the slope, m g sin(angle), accelerates the block.

ideas.title: Bodies tied together share one acceleration
ideas.text: Treat the connected bodies as one system along the line of the rope: net driving force = total mass × acceleration. The tension is internal and cancels. A block that drags another always accelerates at less than g.

ideas.title: A car on a flat curve
ideas.text: Friction alone supplies the inward force, so m v^{2} / R cannot exceed the friction coefficient times m g. The smallest radius is v^{2} / (coefficient × g), and the mass cancels.

ideas.title: Newton's second law
ideas.text: Newton's second law uses the net force. Kinetic friction equals the coefficient times the normal force, and on a level floor with a horizontal pull the normal force equals the weight.

ideas.title: Newton's second law
ideas.text: Resolve the weight along and perpendicular to the slope. Only the component along the slope, m g sin(angle), accelerates the block; the perpendicular component is balanced by the normal force. The mass cancels.

ideas.title: Kinetics of a rigid body
ideas.text: Rotation about a fixed axis follows the rotational form of Newton's second law: net torque = I × angular acceleration. It is the direct counterpart of F = m a.

ideas.title: Newton's second law
ideas.text: On a flat curve friction alone supplies the inward force m v^{2} / R, and friction cannot exceed the coefficient times the weight. Setting the two equal gives the smallest radius, and the mass cancels.

ideas.title: Newton's second law
ideas.text: Bodies joined by a taut cord share one acceleration. Treat them as a single system along the cord: the only driving force is the weight of the hanging block, and it must accelerate the total mass. The tension is internal and cancels.

examples.problem: A 120 kg crate is pulled along a level floor by a 700 N horizontal force. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.35. What is the acceleration of the crate? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.idea: Newton's second law uses the net force. Kinetic friction equals the coefficient times the normal force, and on a level floor with a horizontal pull the normal force equals the weight.

examples.problem: A block slides down a frictionless incline at 35° to the horizontal. What is its acceleration? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.idea: Resolve the weight along and perpendicular to the slope. Only the component along the slope, m g sin(angle), accelerates the block; the perpendicular component is balanced by the normal force. The mass cancels.

figure.svg: <g transform='rotate(-35 200 100)'><line x1='70' y1='120' x2='330' y2='120' stroke='#00242E' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='170' y='80' width='60' height='40' fill='#D9F1D6' stroke='#1B795A' stroke-width='2'/></g><line x1='200' y1='124' x2='200' y2='173' stroke='#00574A' stroke-width='3'/><path d='M200 184 L205 173 L194 173 Z' fill='#00574A'/><text x='208' y='200' text-anchor='start' font-size='11' font-weight='600' fill='#00574A'>W = m g</text><line x1='186' y1='80' x2='158' y2='40' stroke='#1B795A' stroke-width='3'/><path d='M152 31 L154 43 L163 37 Z' fill='#1B795A'/><text x='145' y='25' text-anchor='end' font-size='11' font-weight='600' fill='#1B795A'>N</text><text x='200' y='218' text-anchor='middle' font-size='11' font-weight='400' fill='#00242E'>Only the weight component along the slope, m g sin(angle), causes acceleration</text>
figure.alt: Free-body diagram on a surface inclined at 35° showing W = m g, N.

examples.problem: A net torque of 60 N·m acts on a flywheel with a mass moment of inertia of 8 kg·m^{2}. What is its angular acceleration?
examples.idea: Rotation about a fixed axis follows the rotational form of Newton's second law: net torque = I × angular acceleration. It is the direct counterpart of F = m a.

examples.problem: A car travels at 18 m/s around a flat curve. The coefficient of friction between the tyres and the road is 0.45. What is the smallest radius it can follow without sliding? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.idea: On a flat curve friction alone supplies the inward force m v^{2} / R, and friction cannot exceed the coefficient times the weight. Setting the two equal gives the smallest radius, and the mass cancels.
examples.steps: \frac{m v^{2}}{R} = (coefficient) m g, so R = \frac{v^{2}}{(coefficient) g} = \frac{18^{2}}{0.45(9.81)} = 73.4 m.

figure.svg: <g transform='rotate(0 200 100)'><line x1='70' y1='120' x2='330' y2='120' stroke='#00242E' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='170' y='80' width='60' height='40' fill='#D9F1D6' stroke='#1B795A' stroke-width='2'/></g><line x1='200' y1='124' x2='200' y2='173' stroke='#00574A' stroke-width='3'/><path d='M200 184 L205 173 L194 173 Z' fill='#00574A'/><text x='208' y='200' text-anchor='start' font-size='11' font-weight='600' fill='#00574A'>W</text><line x1='200' y1='76' x2='200' y2='27' stroke='#1B795A' stroke-width='3'/><path d='M200 16 L194 27 L206 27 Z' fill='#1B795A'/><text x='208' y='8' text-anchor='start' font-size='11' font-weight='600' fill='#1B795A'>N</text><line x1='176' y1='100' x2='127' y2='100' stroke='#568CBB' stroke-width='3'/><path d='M116 100 L127 105 L127 94 Z' fill='#568CBB'/><text x='104' y='104' text-anchor='end' font-size='11' font-weight='600' fill='#568CBB'>Friction, toward the centre of the curve</text><text x='200' y='218' text-anchor='middle' font-size='11' font-weight='400' fill='#00242E'>View along the direction of travel</text>
figure.alt: Free-body diagram showing W, N, Friction, toward the centre of the curve.

examples.problem: A 9 kg block on a frictionless table is tied by a cord over a light, frictionless pulley to a hanging 3 kg block. What is the acceleration of the blocks? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.idea: Bodies joined by a taut cord share one acceleration. Treat them as a single system along the cord: the only driving force is the weight of the hanging block, and it must accelerate the total mass. The tension is internal and cancels.
examples.steps:
Driving force = 3(9.81) = 29.43 N. Total mass = 9 + 3 = 12 kg.

a = \frac{29.43}{12} = 2.45 m/s^{2}, which is less than g as it must be.

examples.problem: A 72 kg person stands on a scale in a lift that is accelerating upward at 1.4 m/s^{2}. What force does the scale read? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.idea: The scale reads the normal force. Newton's second law for the person, with upward positive, is N - m g = m a, so the reading exceeds the weight while the lift accelerates upward.

sections.deep:
Newton's second law links forces to motion: the net force equals mass times acceleration, in each direction separately. For rotation about a fixed axis the net moment equals the mass moment of inertia times the angular acceleration.

The free-body diagram is as essential here as in statics; the difference is that the forces no longer sum to zero. Friction uses the kinetic coefficient once the body is moving. In U.S. customary units, mass is weight divided by g.
method: Draw the free-body diagram and choose axes along and across the direction of motion.
Write the sum of forces = m a along the motion and the sum of forces = 0 across it.
Find the normal force first when friction is involved.
Solve for acceleration, then use kinematics for speed, distance or time.
For rotation, write the sum of moments = I × angular acceleration about the fixed axis.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: Newton's second law says a net force makes a mass accelerate: force = mass × acceleration. Draw the free-body diagram, add the forces in the direction of motion, and set the total equal to mass times acceleration. For rotation, net moment = mass moment of inertia × angular acceleration.
sections.work: The curve design formula for superelevation and side friction is Newton's second law for a vehicle turning.
terms: free-body diagram
a sketch of one object on its own with every force acting on it drawn as an arrow; the first step of almost every force problem
moment
the turning effect of a force about a point: the force times its perpendicular distance from that point
mass moment of inertia
a body's resistance to being spun up or slowed down about an axis
normal force
the force a surface exerts perpendicular to itself on an object resting or pressing on it
symbols: acceleration due to gravity, 9.81 m/s^{2} (32.2 ft/s^{2})

sections.title: Work, energy and power
sections.body:
Work is force times the distance moved in the direction of the force. Energy is the ability to do work. Kinetic energy belongs to motion, and potential energy is stored in height or in a stretched spring.

If only gravity and springs act, total mechanical energy stays the same, so you can jump straight from the start to the finish without tracking time. Friction removes energy equal to the friction force times the distance. Power is the rate of doing work. Impulse and momentum handle impacts: force times time equals the change in mass times velocity.

formulas.name: Work-energy
formulas.expr: work done = change in kinetic energy

pitfalls: Forgetting that speed is squared in kinetic energy: doubling speed quadruples the energy.
Using energy methods when the question asks for time.
Using the moment of inertia about the centre of mass in the kinetic energy of a body that rotates about a pin.

example.problem: A 1,000 kg car moving at 20 m/s brakes to a stop. How much energy do the brakes absorb?

ideas.title: Energy for a swinging body
ideas.text: For a body rotating about a pin, the potential energy lost is m g times the drop of its centre of mass, and the kinetic energy gained is one half of the moment of inertia about the pin times the angular speed squared.

ideas.title: Conservation of energy
ideas.text: With no air resistance, mechanical energy is conserved: m g h of potential energy becomes (1/2) m v^{2} of kinetic energy. The mass cancels, so v = square root of 2 g h for any object.

ideas.title: Power and efficiency
ideas.text: Power is force times velocity in the direction of the force. At constant speed the hoist force equals the weight, so P = m g v.

ideas.title: Elastic potential energy
ideas.text: Energy is conserved: the elastic energy stored in the spring, (1/2) k x^{2}, becomes the kinetic energy of the block, (1/2) m v^{2}.

ideas.title: Work and energy
ideas.text: Energy is conserved. The rod's centre of mass falls by L / 2, and that potential energy becomes rotational kinetic energy about the pin, where the rod's moment of inertia is m L^{2} / 3.

examples.problem: A 4 kg ball is dropped from rest from a height of 30 m. Ignoring air resistance, how fast is it moving just before it lands? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.idea: With no air resistance, mechanical energy is conserved: m g h of potential energy becomes (1/2) m v^{2} of kinetic energy. The mass cancels, so v = square root of 2 g h for any object.
examples.steps: m g h = \frac{1}{2} m v^{2}, so v = \sqrt{2 g h} = \sqrt{2(9.81)(30)} = 24.3 m/s. The 4 kg mass is not needed.

examples.problem: A hoist lifts a 2,000 kg load at a constant 1.2 m/s. What power is delivered to the load? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.idea: Power is force times velocity in the direction of the force. At constant speed the hoist force equals the weight, so P = m g v.

figure.alt: Free-body diagram showing Weight = m g, Cable force = m g at constant speed.

examples.problem: A spring with a stiffness of 3,000 N/m is compressed 0.12 m and released against a 1.5 kg block on a frictionless surface. What speed does the block reach?
examples.idea: Energy is conserved: the elastic energy stored in the spring, (1/2) k x^{2}, becomes the kinetic energy of the block, (1/2) m v^{2}.

examples.problem: A uniform slender rod 1.8 m long is released from rest in a horizontal position and swings about a frictionless pin at one end. What is its angular speed as it passes through the vertical? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.idea: Energy is conserved. The rod's centre of mass falls by L / 2, and that potential energy becomes rotational kinetic energy about the pin, where the rod's moment of inertia is m L^{2} / 3.
examples.steps: m g \frac{L}{2} = \frac{1}{2}(\frac{m L^{2}}{3})(angular speed)^{2}, so angular speed = \sqrt{\frac{3 g}{L}} = \sqrt{\frac{3(9.81)}{1.8}} = 4.04 rad/s.

examples.problem: A car travelling at 22 m/s locks its wheels on a level road where the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.57. How far does it slide before stopping? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.idea: The work done by friction equals the kinetic energy removed: (coefficient) m g d = (1/2) m v^{2}. The mass cancels, and the distance grows with the square of the speed.

figure.alt: Free-body diagram showing W, N, Friction = (coefficient) N.

examples.problem: A 18,750 kg truck climbs a 6% grade at a steady 15 m/s. Ignoring rolling and air resistance, what power does the climb require? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.idea: Power is force times speed. At steady speed the driving force equals the weight component along the slope, m g times the grade as a decimal (for small slopes the sine equals the grade).

sections.deep:
Energy methods relate speeds to positions without solving for acceleration or time. The work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy. When only gravity and springs act, mechanical energy is conserved: kinetic plus gravitational potential plus elastic potential is constant. Friction removes energy equal to the friction force times the sliding distance.

Power is the rate of doing work, force times velocity. Efficiency is output power over input power. Impulse and momentum handle forces acting over time and collisions, where momentum is conserved and the coefficient of restitution sets the rebound.
method: Choose the two states to compare and a datum for height.
Write kinetic, gravitational and spring energy at each state.
Add work done by non-conservative forces (friction is negative).
Solve the energy balance for the unknown speed or distance.
For impact, write conservation of momentum, then the restitution equation.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: Work is force times the distance moved along it. Doing work on an object changes its kinetic energy, the energy of motion. Raising it stores potential energy. Power is how fast work is done. Tracking energy often avoids having to find acceleration.
terms: kinetic energy
energy of motion: half the mass times the speed squared
momentum
mass times velocity; a force acting for a time changes it
moment
the turning effect of a force about a point: the force times its perpendicular distance from that point
symbols: acceleration due to gravity, 9.81 m/s^{2} (32.2 ft/s^{2})
